title: Bishop and queen from board A mate on board B
summary: On board B, Black lost the queen early to a rook won on board A, and from then on queens and rooks kept crossing between the boards. The finish came from board A: A-White's Qxd3+ sent the bishop for B@d2+ and Qxf5+ sent the queen for Q@e3#. Watch move 18 on board A, where Black checks with N@e3+ first so that taking the queen on e5 would not hand B-Black a mating queen.
event: HypeBeast 1.1.1 (pre-release build) against HypeBeast 1.1.0, 500,000 nodes a move

result.text: Black on board B mates; the team of A-White and B-Black wins.

moves.note: The bishop comes from board B, where Nxd2 had just taken B-Black's bishop. The engine first chose B@d5, then a longer look within the same move switched it to B@g6. The drops it compared came out almost level overall, with or without the pawn it expected from board B, and a pawn did arrive soon after, from fxe3. Taking on d3 at once was what a search that ignores the other board wanted; Black played Nxd3+ on its next move.

lines.note: White answers Nc5 and later takes the new bishop with Bxg6.
The first choice, B@d5, from the game's own search.
A search that ignores the other board takes on d3 at once; searched the same way, this scored worse for Black than B@g6.
Had the pawn already arrived, the engine's plan was B@f5.

moves.note: The knight from N@c2+ takes the rook on a1, and the rook goes straight to B-White, who drops it with R@f3 next move against the queen on f6. By A-Black's count this capture was worth more for what the rook would do on board B than on board A.
The rook from board A takes B-Black's queen. That queen goes to A-Black, who keeps it in hand until Q@d6. B-Black answers at once with Nxa4, taking White's queen for A-White.

Its first choice was Nc5. It dropped the knight on b7 instead, attacking the queen on d8, and Nxd8 won it on its next move. By the engine's count one more queen for B-Black was enough to mate on board B; the queen arrived and was dropped as Q@a1+, though no mate came of it.

The queen B-Black won with Nxa4 comes back in on e5, facing Black's queen on d6. Its first choice was Nxe6; it switched because it expected a knight from board B, about five chances in six, and with a knight in hand Q@e5 scored better. The knight came, from Qxf6. Black's N@e3+ is the answer to this drop.

B-Black's queen, the one won on board A with Nxd8, takes the knight that had checked from f6, and that knight goes to A-White. Rxf6 then takes the queen, which goes to A-Black. The engine scored this exchange well in its favour, and the other recapture, gxf6, far worse. By its next move here it scored itself about three pawns down; in between, Qxe5 on board A had sent White a queen.

lines.note: Playing White's side itself, the engine expected Rxf6 and still scored Black well ahead.
White's own engine, choosing Rxf6, scored the position about twelve pawns in White's favour: the two engines disagreed about this exchange.

moves.note: Its first choice was Qxe5, taking the queen A-White had just dropped. But White's queen on e2 would take back on e5 and send Black's queen to B-Black, who by the engine's count could then mate with Q@d2 on board B unless B-White acted in time. So it checks first with N@e3+. After dxe3 the pawn on e3 stands between White's queen and e5, and Black took the queen with Qxe5 on its next move; the knight went to B-Black.

lines.note: After dxe3 Qxe5, White replies Qxc2 rather than taking back on e5.
The first choice: Qxe5 Qxe5, the exchange that would send Black's queen to B-Black.
A search that ignores the other board plays Nd4; searched the same way, it scored about the same as N@e3+.
With the queen it expected from board B already in hand, its plan was to take on e5 and check with Q@d1+.

moves.note: Now Black takes the queen, which goes to B-White, who drops it later as Q@d3. On board A alone the engine scored this about level, yet its total was about 26 pawns for White: by its count, a White capture of a queen, bishop or pawn here would let B-Black mate. Its line begins Nxe6, and White did take the bishop on e6 next move; B-Black dropped it as B@g7.

lines.note: The engine's line: White takes the bishop with Nxe6 and then the knight on c2 with Qxc2.
A search that ignores the other board plays Bxd3; searched the same way, it scored worse for Black than Qxe5.

moves.note: Its first choice was Nf2. It took the rook on f6 instead, sending it to A-White, because it expected a queen from board A, about five chances in six, and with a queen in hand Bxf6 scored far better. The queen came, from Rxd8+, but by its next move here its score had fallen, and a search with four times the work preferred N@f2. The rook it sent stayed in A-White's hand until R@f4+, the last check on board A.

lines.note: White takes back with Bxf6.
The first choice, Nf2, from the game's own search.
A search that ignores the other board plays d6; searched the same way, it scored better for Black than Bxf6.
Four times the work prefers N@f2, a line ending with Nxd3+ taking White's queen; it scored better for Black than Bxf6.
White's own engine after Bxf6 scored White about six pawns ahead.
With the queen already in hand, its plan was N@c3 and later Q@b2+.

moves.note: The queen won by Rxd8+ on board A goes straight in with check. Qxd2 is White's only move, and it sends that queen to A-Black; exd2+ then takes White's queen for A-White and leaves a pawn checking from d2. The engine's other tries scored much worse by its count.

lines.note: The engine's line; the game followed it until White took the knight with Kxd1 instead of Kxd2.

moves.note: Taking the bishop with check also sends it to B-Black, who used it for B@d2+ near the end. By the engine's count most of this score was what its captures would give B-Black: on board A alone it was only about two pawns up, and a short search found that one more queen in B-Black's hand was enough to mate there. A search that ignores the other board preferred R@d1.

lines.note: The engine's line goes on to take the knight on c2 with Qxc2 as well.
A search that ignores the other board drops a rook on d1; searched the same way it scored better on board A, but that search counts nothing of what the bishop is worth on board B.
Had A-Black received a pawn first, its plan was N@c5+.

moves.note: The only legal move: the knight on f2 gives check. By White's next decision its score had gone from about level to more than twenty pawns down, after B-Black's N@c4+, but there was nothing to choose here. The pawn taken on d2 went to A-Black.

lines.note: White's own line, which it scored about level.
B-Black's plan at its next move, Ne4+ with B@f4+ to follow, scored about nine pawns up for Black; it played N@c4+ instead.

moves.note: Its first choice was Ne4+. It dropped its other knight with N@c4+ instead, because if queens were traded on board A, which it gave about one chance in five, this check led to a forced mate by its count, while without a trade the two checks scored about the same. Two moves later A-White's Qxf5+ sent the queen.

lines.note: After Ke1, as played, the engine scored Black far ahead.
The first choice, Ne4+, with B@f4+ to follow.

moves.note: The bishop A-White sent with Qxd3+ comes in with check, and the engine now saw mate in two. Kxf2 is White's only move, and the queen that A-White's Qxf5+ has just sent is waiting for Q@e3#.

lines.note: Kxf2, the only move, and the queen drop on e3 mates.

moves.note: The queen A-White won with Qxf5+ on board A mates. B-White had received a queen too, from Kxf5, but its only move in between was the forced Kxf2. On board A, A-White was checking with R@f4+, the rook B-Black had sent with Bxf6, and by its own count had mate in three there.
